children: Quess CFO says the company’s financial strategy is shifting from balance-sheet stabilisation to deciding where capital should be deployed and what returns it should generate

As staffing companies globally position AI-augmented workforce management as their next growth driver, the industry faces a structural question: does AI reinforce a business built on headcount, or work against it? Neeraj Jain, Chief Financial Officer of Quess Corp, addresses that tension alongside the company's FY26 financial performance, its capital-allocation approach following the three-way demerger into Quess Corp, Digitide Solutions and Bluspring Enterprises, and the balance between shareholder returns and growth investment under its ‘Quess 2.0’ strategy.

Quess Corp's FY26 revenue grew 2 per cent to Rs 15,305 crore, while EBITDA jumped 19 per cent to Rs 312 crore, with margin expansion outpacing top-line growth. What's actually driving that gap: cost discipline post-demerger, a shift towards higher-margin segments, or something structural in how the staffing business now operates?

The divergence between revenue and EBITDA growth reflects a combination of better cost discipline and a healthier business mix. Over the year, some of our higher-margin businesses have grown faster and contributed more meaningfully to profitability, while we have also remained focused on operating efficiency at the corporate level.

To put numbers to it: Professional Staffing revenue grew 13 per cent, with EBITDA margin expanding from 9.3 per cent to 11.9 per cent, and our overseas business grew 5 per cent, with margin improving from 5.5 per cent to 6.4 per cent. General Staffing, still around 86 per cent of revenue, remains a large and important part of the portfolio, and within this business we are increasingly focusing on higher-value, better-margin opportunities across areas such as construction, manufacturing and value-added services.

Professional Staffing and Overseas are growing faster and carrying a disproportionate share of the profit improvement relative to their share of revenue, which is the real driver of the gap between our revenue and EBITDA growth.
We are increasingly measuring growth on quality of revenue, margin profile and operating leverage rather than only on topline expansion, and that is what lets profitability grow faster than revenue.

Quess has committed to returning roughly 75 per cent of free cash flow to shareholders over three years, having just gone net-cash and repaid its gross debt. How do you balance that shareholder-return commitment against funding the ‘Quess 2.0’ growth and AI ambitions? Are those two promises compatible, or is one going to give?
We see shareholder returns and investment in Quess 2.0 as complementary priorities within a disciplined capital-allocation framework.

For us, Quess 2.0 means four things: deepening our core business with a stronger focus on value alongside volume, building international mobility corridors, supporting GCCs end-to-end, and driving AI-led productivity across the business.

Our approach is to balance three things: returning capital to shareholders, investing in technology and AI-led capabilities that improve the core business, and selectively pursuing inorganic growth where there is a clear strategic and financial fit.

We assess every opportunity, whether it is a shareholder return or a growth investment, against the same principles: expected returns, cash generation and long-term value creation. We ended FY26 with a net cash position of Rs 271 crore, an ROE of 20 per cent and EBITDA-to-operating-cash-flow conversion of 80 per cent, and that balance sheet strength is what lets us keep investing in Quess 2.0 while honouring our 75 per cent free-cash-flow return commitment.

You joined as CFO months after Quess's three-way demerger into Quess Corp, Digitide Solutions and Bluspring Enterprises. How much of your first year has been about stabilising a newly ‘focused’ balance sheet versus setting new financial strategy, and how do you tell the difference?
The first phase naturally involved ensuring that the post-demerger organisation had a clean financial foundation, appropriate governance structures and a disciplined capital framework.

But stabilisation is only useful if it creates the platform for the next stage. The more important work now is building the financial architecture for Quess 2.0, how we think about returns on capital, cash conversion, investment priorities and the quality of growth.

Concretely, FY26 was the year we became debt-free and closed with Rs 271 crore of net cash, alongside a 20 per cent ROE and 80 per cent EBITDA-to-cash conversion. The work now is deploying that strength deliberately, against a clear return threshold, rather than simply repairing the balance sheet.
For me, the distinction is fairly simple: stabilisation is about removing legacy complexity; strategy is about deciding where the next rupee of capital should go and what return we expect from it.
How do you make the financial case for AI investment in a business where AI's success could shrink the metric your revenue has always been built on?

Our economics depend more on how efficiently we source, deploy and administer talent against client demand than on how many people we add. Our aspiration is to be a tech-first company, and AI is increasingly being embedded across the way we operate, from sourcing and recruiter productivity to associate servicing and back-end processes. AI has the potential to improve that operating model by increasing recruiter productivity, automating repetitive processes and improving the conversion of open mandates into productive, billable associates.

The financial case for AI rests on reducing friction, improving fulfilment and lowering our cost-to-serve, while keeping the workforce base intact. There is also a balance-sheet dimension that gets less attention: automating processes like timesheet validation and purchase-order matching directly reduces unbilled revenue and shortens our working-capital cycle, which is a meaningful and immediate financial benefit from AI, independent of any headcount question.
Is the industry's AI narrative a genuine reinvention of the staffing model, or a way of reassuring investors while headcount-billing quietly erodes?

In India, staffing is still being shaped by a much more fundamental structural trend, the formalisation of a very large informal workforce. In many frontline and blue-collar categories, the constraint is not an absence of demand; it is the ability to source and fulfil demand efficiently.

In that context, AI is more immediately relevant as an operating-efficiency and fill-rate tool than as a replacement for the staffing model itself. Over time, technology will certainly change how staffing companies operate, but the more important question is whether it improves productivity, client outcomes and returns. That is the lens through which we evaluate it.

We are seeing this play out in our own technology staffing business too. A growing share of the roles our GCC clients are asking us to fill sit in AI, machine learning and data specialisations. Our latest GCC Tech Talent report shows that demand across AI, data and cloud roles grew around 10 per cent quarter-on-quarter, underscoring how quickly these capabilities are moving up the hiring agenda. That shift is one of the reasons Professional Staffing has been able to grow both revenue and margin faster than the rest of the business.
